title: Health & well-being: yours and the team's
blurb: Recognising stress and burnout, coping strategies, breaks, occupational health, where to get support, and looking after your colleagues.
question: For weeks you've been skipping breaks to keep a packed list on time. You're sleeping badly and last week you mislabelled a set of radiographs. A colleague seems just as exhausted. What should you do for yourself, and how could you support your colleague?

teach.h: Your well-being is a patient-safety issue
teach.body: Tired, stressed or unwell staff make more mistakes and are more likely to be injured. That's why one of the nine duties of a dental nurse is to manage your own health and well-being and promote the well-being of others in the team. Well-being covers your physical health, such as your back, your hands and your immunisations, and your mental health, such as stress, anxiety and burnout.

Stress is your response to pressure that feels more than you can cope with. Short bursts of pressure can be motivating, but long-term stress harms health. Burnout is a state of exhaustion caused by long-term work stress: you feel emotionally drained, detached or cynical about work, and less effective. In dentistry, common causes include heavy workloads, running late and difficult patients. The HSE's Management Standards group the main causes of work stress into six areas: demands, control, support, relationships, role and change.

bands.label: Burnt out: exhausted, detached, can't cope

teach.caption: An informal self-check, not a clinical tool. The earlier you act, the easier it is to recover.

teach.h: Act early and ask for help
teach.body: If you feel overwhelmed or start making mistakes, raise it with your manager and seek support rather than carrying on silently. Coping strategies that help include reflection, accepting that you won't get everything right, debriefing after a difficult event, handing over to a colleague when you need to, peer support and simply asking for help. Look after the basics too: breaks, sleep, food, exercise and time away from work. If your health could affect patient safety, you must seek advice and adjust your work.

teach.caption: Some employers also offer an employee assistance programme, and indemnity providers and professional associations often run support lines.

items.label: rest break if you work more than 6 hours in a day
average maximum working week (you can opt out)

teach.caption: Working Time Regulations 1998, for adult workers. Fatigue increases the risk of errors and injuries such as sharps injuries.

teach.body: If a colleague seems exhausted or is making errors, speak to them privately and kindly, listen, and encourage them to seek support. Don't gossip about it or ignore it. After a stressful event such as a medical emergency, a team debrief helps everyone process it and learn. Change, like a new computer system, can be unsettling: asking questions, asking for training and focusing on what you can control all help.

Occupational health advises on whether you are fit for work, supports a safe return after illness or injury, recommends reasonable adjustments and manages sharps injuries and immunisations such as hepatitis B. Look after your body: adjust your chair, keep a neutral posture and stretch between patients to protect your back and neck. Report sore, cracked hands early, as dermatitis from frequent hand hygiene and gloves is common and treatable.

teach.text: Working through breaks to keep the list on time isn't dedication: fatigue raises the risk of errors and injury. Discuss the pressure and agree a workable plan with your manager.

items: Your well-being affects patient safety; the team's well-being is everyone's job.
Burnout: emotional exhaustion, detachment, feeling ineffective.
Overwhelmed or making mistakes? Raise it with your manager and seek support.
Coping: reflection, self-acceptance, debriefing, handing over, peer support, asking for help.
Take breaks: 20 minutes if working over 6 hours. Fatigue causes errors and injuries.
Exhausted colleague: speak privately, listen, encourage support. Occupational health for work-related health.

summary: You can now recognise the signs of stress and burnout in yourself and others, choose healthy coping strategies, explain why breaks matter, know where to get support including occupational health, and respond kindly and professionally to a struggling colleague.

A.q: A dental nurse feels constantly overwhelmed and has started making uncharacteristic mistakes. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Keep going quietly and hope it passes
Raise it with the manager and seek support
Take on extra shifts to catch up on the backlog
A.why: Raising it early with the manager and seeking support protects both the nurse and patients.

whyNot.0: Carrying on silently risks more mistakes and worsening health.
whyNot.2: Resigning is a big decision that doesn't address the support they need now.
whyNot.3: More work will make exhaustion and mistakes worse.

A.q: Why should a dental nurse take regular breaks during long clinical sessions?
options: Breaks only matter if the dentist agrees
It makes the list finish earlier
Fatigue raises the risk of errors and injury
Breaks are optional for clinical staff on busy lists
A.why: Fatigue increases the risk of mistakes and injuries such as sharps injuries.

whyNot.0: Rest breaks are a legal entitlement, not a favour.
whyNot.1: Breaks don't shorten the list; they keep you safe.
whyNot.3: Adult workers are entitled to rest breaks under the Working Time Regulations.

A.q: You notice a colleague looks exhausted and has made several errors this week. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report them to the GDC straight away
Mention it to the whole team over lunch
Say nothing, as it isn't your business
A.why: A private, kind conversation encouraging them to seek support is the right first step.

whyNot.0: Going straight to the regulator is disproportionate for exhaustion with no wider concern.
whyNot.1: Discussing a colleague with others is unkind and breaks trust.
whyNot.2: Ignoring it leaves your colleague struggling and patients at risk.

B.q: Which is a recognised sign of burnout?
options: Feeling energised by a new challenge
Enjoying a busy but manageable day
B.why: Burnout is marked by emotional exhaustion, detachment or cynicism, and feeling less effective.

whyNot.0: Feeling energised is a sign of healthy pressure.
whyNot.2: A manageable busy day is normal, healthy work.

B.q: A dental nurse has sore, cracked hands that aren't improving. Who is best placed to assess this as a work-related condition?
B.why: Occupational health assesses work-related conditions such as dermatitis and advises on adjustments.

whyNot.0: Receptionists aren't trained to assess health conditions.
whyNot.1: The GDC regulates professionals; it doesn't assess staff health.
whyNot.3: A sales rep can't assess a health condition.

B.q: After a stressful medical emergency in the practice, what is a helpful coping strategy for the team?
options: A team debrief to talk it through
B.why: Debriefing helps the team process what happened, support each other and learn.

whyNot.0: Avoiding it can leave people distressed and lessons unlearned.
whyNot.1: Blame damages the team and stops honest learning.
whyNot.2: Overworking adds to stress rather than relieving it.

C.q: You're asked to work through your break again to keep a packed list on time. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree every time to avoid causing a fuss
Refuse, and walk out of the surgery
Discuss the pressure and agree a plan
Skip lunch, but take longer tomorrow
C.why: Raising the pressure on the list and agreeing a workable plan protects you and patients.

whyNot.0: Always agreeing leads to fatigue and errors.
whyNot.1: Walking out leaves patients and colleagues unsupported.
whyNot.3: Rest can't be banked; you need breaks on the day you work.

C.q: Under the Working Time Regulations, what rest break is an adult worker entitled to when working more than six hours in a day?
C.why: Adult workers are entitled to an uninterrupted 20-minute rest break when working more than six hours.

whyNot.0: Ten minutes is below the legal minimum.
whyNot.2: Employers may give more, but the legal minimum is 20 minutes.
whyNot.3: An hour may be offered by contract, but the legal minimum is 20 minutes.

C.q: The practice is moving to a new computer system and a nurse feels anxious about the change. Which strategy is most helpful?
options: Avoid it until others have learned it
Insist on keeping the old system
C.why: Asking questions and getting training reduces uncertainty and builds confidence with change.

whyNot.1: Avoiding the change makes it harder later.
whyNot.2: Resisting change doesn't help her adapt.
whyNot.3: Bottling up worry adds to stress.

reteach.title: Think of your phone battery
reteach.question: Your phone warns you at 20% and dies at 0%. What does a battery teach you about looking after yourself at work?

blocks.body: You can't run all day on 2%. Breaks, sleep and time off are your charger. The low-battery warning is like your warning signs: poor sleep, irritability, mistakes. The sensible thing is to plug in early, by talking to your manager or GP, not to wait until you shut down. And if a colleague's battery is flashing red, you lend them your charger: a kind word, a listening ear and encouragement to get support.

blocks.h: What to do at each level

steps.label: Half
steps.sub: Talk to a colleague; protect your breaks

steps.label: Low
steps.sub: Tell your manager; see OH or your GP

steps.label: Empty
steps.sub: Get urgent help: GP, NHS 111, Samaritans

explain.body: Watch for poor sleep, irritability, uncharacteristic mistakes, withdrawal and skipping breaks. Burnout adds emotional exhaustion, detachment and feeling ineffective.

test.q: Which is an early warning sign of stress in yourself?
options: Looking forward to going to work
Taking all your breaks on time
test.why: Irritability and uncharacteristic mistakes are common early signs of stress.

whyNot.1: Good sleep is a sign of coping well.
whyNot.2: Looking forward to work suggests healthy well-being.
whyNot.3: Taking breaks is a protective habit.

explain.body: Healthy coping strategies include reflection, self-acceptance, debriefing, handing over to a colleague, peer support and asking for help.

head: Strategy
Example
rows: Swap a task when you're struggling
A trusted colleague to talk to

test.q: Which is a healthy coping strategy for dental professionals?
test.why: Peer support is a recognised healthy coping strategy.

whyNot.0: Hiding mistakes increases stress and risk.
whyNot.3: Isolation makes stress harder to manage.

explain.body: At work: your manager or mentor. Occupational health: fitness for work, adjustments, injuries, immunisations. Your GP for your own health. Urgent help: NHS 111, 999 or Samaritans.

test.q: A nurse needs advice on returning to work safely after an injury, possibly with adjustments. Who is most appropriate?
test.why: Occupational health advises on fitness for work, safe return and reasonable adjustments.

whyNot.0: The CQC inspects services, not individual staff health.
whyNot.2: Patients shouldn't be asked for health advice about staff.
whyNot.3: A technician has no role in staff health.

explain.body: Notice the signs, speak privately and kindly, listen without judging, encourage them to seek support and check in later.

test.q: A colleague tells you they are struggling and not sleeping. What should you do?
options: Tell the whole team so they can all help out
Tell them everyone feels like that
Advise them to resign straight away
Listen and encourage them to get support
test.why: Listening and encouraging them to seek support is kind and appropriate.

whyNot.0: Sharing without consent breaks their trust.
whyNot.1: Dismissing their feelings may stop them seeking help.
whyNot.2: Resigning isn't a solution you should push on them.
